highlights.title: ‘Smart’ Nanoparticles Deliver mRNA Directly to Tumors in New Cancer Therapy
highlights.summary: The treatment can reprogram immune cells that have been corrupted by the cancer, strengthening the body’s ability to attack.
body: Our immune systems don’t just fight bacteria and viruses invading the body. They are responsible for keeping our own tissues in check, taking out cancerous cells before they have a chance to grow. Once a tumor forms, however, it can create an environment that declaws cancer-fighting immune cells—in some cases even reprogramming them to suppress other parts of the immune system.

Overcoming the oppressive tumor environment remains a barrier for even some of the most promising treatments. “One of the biggest challenges in cancer immunotherapy is that the immune system may be capable of attacking a tumor, but the tumor environment can stop those immune cells from doing their job,” University of Adelaide professor Chunxia Zhao explained in a press release.
points: The treatment can reprogram immune cells that have been corrupted by the cancer, strengthening the body’s ability to attack.

highlights.title: Measure by measure, studying society accurately
highlights.summary: Naoki Egami has become a standout in political methodology, helping refine tools that give scholars durable results.
body: Images for download on the MIT News office website are made available to non-commercial entities, press and the general public under a Creative Commons Attribution Non-Commercial No Derivatives license. You may not alter the images provided, other than to crop them to size. A credit line must be used when reproducing images; if one is not provided below, credit the images to "MIT."
Let’s agree at the outset the world is a complicated place, and social scientists have exacting jobs when it comes to measuring civic phenomena with precision.

After all, even careful studies raise follow-up questions: How much do their findings apply in other settings? Do conclusions about politics in one country apply to other countries? If you’re studying voters in a lopsided election, will your findings apply to voters in a close election? Those questions are all a natural part of the research process.

That’s where Naoki Egami comes in. Egami is an MIT political scientist whose specialty is the methodology of research. He carefully scrutinizes, for one thing, what social scientists call “external validity,” whether the results of particular studies apply more generally.

highlights.title: Login errors delay Diablo 4's big new Season of Hell's Legacy anniversary update
highlights.summary: The launch of Diablo 4 's Season of Hell's Legacy got off to a rough start. The anticipated season was announced at BlizzCon over the weekend to arrive alongside a 30th anniversary celebration of the Diablo franchise.
body: Players reported running into a number of login issues, with error codes 300006 and 300008 the most commonly reported. "We're aware of an issue preventing some players from accessing Diablo 4. The team is actively investigating and working to resolve the issue as quickly as possible," was the Diablo account's immediate response on X.

Two hours later, the Diablo account posted another update announcing the season launch delay, and Diablo 4 was entirely inaccessible throughout that period and for hours later. "We're continuing to address issues affecting today's launch of Season of Hell's Legacy. As a result, Season 15 is currently delayed. We appreciate your patience while we work to resolve the issues and we'll share updates as we have them."

It took another two hours for things to approve, with Blizzard confirming log in issues had been resolved, but some game features had to be temporarily disabled. The season ended up going live over six hours later.

body: “ La Bola Negra,” Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi ’s Cannes Festival sensation, is Spain’s submission for the 2027 international feature film Academy Award.
Any other Oscar entry choice from Spain than “La Bola Negra,” announced Wednesday by Alejandro Amenábar on behalf of Spain’s Academia de Cine, would have been a huge shock.
The choice came after a second-round vote by Academy members, following the Sept. 3 selection of “La Bola Negra,” “The Beloved” and “Sundays” as the country’s three shortlisted titles.

World premiering in Cannes main competition, “La Bola Negra” first caught attention by scoring a 16 minute standing ovation at its world premiere on the Croisette. It caused a further splash winning best director, shared with Paweł Pawlikowski for “Fatherland.”

highlights.title: The other side of Croatia: ‘a landscape that could out-Tuscany Tuscany’
highlights.summary: Weekenders from Zagreb head to the rolling green Samobor Hills for nature, vineyards, delicious local food and Habsburg-era architecture. ‘You’re going to Samobor? You must try kremšnita,” my Dubrovnik friends told me before I set off on my trip north.
body: It lived up to the hype – delicately rich, creamy and with a light touch. After spending a few weeks in sun-bleached Venetian Dalmatia, amid the scrubby, limestone Dinaric Alps, I had swapped empires and was firmly in Habsburg Croatia. Here, in Zagreb County’s prettiest town, handsome baroque houses in pastel shades of buttery yellow, apricot and pistachio, festooned with stucco, line narrow King Tomislav Square, whose umbrella-shaded cafe terraces were filled with Croatians getting their morning fix of coffee and chatter.

As well as the graceful architectural legacy of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, this rolling green landscape is crisscrossed with forested trails, particularly within the Žumberak nature park, about 16 miles (26km) west of Samobor, where weekenders from Zagreb come to hike and bike in woods of hornbeam, oak and beech with bubbling waterfalls. Not having time for a full-on hike, I could still drive to Potočna dolina Slapnica, near the Vranjak waterfalls, and scramble up the path beside a series of cascades each more impressive than the last.

highlights.title: Age Limits for Social Media Outlined by European Union
highlights.summary: Teens using their phones in Valence, France, this summer. The EU Kids Act would restrict social media use for children under 15.
body: The proposal, called the EU Kids Act, would bar children under the age of 13 from using social media, Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, the bloc’s executive branch, said in a speech in Strasbourg, France. Teens aged 13 and 14 could access new “mini accounts” supervised by parents that would limit their contact with strangers and overall screen time. Access to a more independent account would be allowed from age 15.
“It is not about our minors accessing social media. It is about when and how do we allow social media to access minors,” said Ms. von der Leyen during an annual State of the Union address.

The act would be one of the biggest policy steps to date in a global movement to limit children’s screen time and access to social media. The European Union, home to 450 million people, has long been an aggressive regulator of the tech industry, using its power to force companies to change products and policies. In recent years, Apple changed its App Store, Google its search engine and Meta its data-privacy practices to comply with European laws and regulations.
points: The EU Kids Act would restrict social media use for children under 15.

highlights.title: AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular in every poll
highlights.summary: Poll data released Tuesday by the New York Times and Siena University confirms what we've already been seeing, and what politicians are responding to - AI and data centers are incredibly unpopular.
body: 61 percent of likely voters said they oppose the construction of AI data centers, but neither major party has much of an edge.

56 percent of voters surveyed who said they were opposed to data centers said they supported limits, while 38 percent instead preferred a total ban. The list of reasons for opposition is also revealing, with the environment/water usage most common at 32 percent, impact on local communities at 21 percent, general distrust or dislike of AI at 18 percent, followed by regulation concerns and the economy at 10 and 9 percent.
An NBC News poll in March showed AI polling lower than ICE, and a Gallup poll in May revealed seven in ten Americans opposed local construction of AI data centers.

highlights.summary: Baldur’s Gate 3 is full of moments like this: A great character, an intriguing story, and then no reliable way to learn what happens next. For Mizora — Wyll's patron devil, the one who granted him his warlock powers — a new mod has delivered a way around that issue.
body: A frustrating scene for your consideration: A paladin leads his people out of a burning camp, holds together the survivors of a massacre, and fights off Absolute cultists not once but twice…and then you just say goodbye? Here’s another: A druid nearly gets an entire grove slaughtered, spends the rest of the story trying to live with the consequences, and the game decides that's not compelling enough to keep them around. Excuse me?!
Why we’re inviting Alfira to camp: One song from her was simply never going to be enough.
Why we’re inviting Barcus to camp: He survived three acts of hell and still doesn't get a spot at the campfire?

Barcus is a gnome you rescue from a burning windmill early in Act 1, if you’re so inclined. After that, his life doesn’t exactly get easier. He’s captured (again), he’s tortured for information about his former friend Wulbren's whereabouts, dragged to Moonrise Towers, and finally handed leadership of the Ironhand clan in Act 3 after everyone else in charge lets him down. His arc gives him as much story as a companion — he just needs a class to build skills around. After everything he’s been through, he’s earned at least that much.

highlights.title: A moment that changed me: I felt hugely self conscious about my skin - until I had a revelation
highlights.summary: For years, my vitiligo controlled my life, and I was constantly trying to disguise it. But one day, I realised I could take a very different and extremely liberating approach. The microphone felt heavier than I expected.
body: I was three years old when I developed my first patch of vitiligo on the back of my hand, which later spread to my arms, legs, face and other parts of my body. By the time I was six years old, 70% of me was covered. I was too young to understand what was happening.

Despite this, I had a happy childhood because I was unaware then that being different was something that was viewed negatively. I went swimming, wore shorts and T-shirts, and barely gave my skin much thought. My parents taught me it was part of me and that it wasn’t something that had to hold me back. However, what I couldn’t foresee was how others would perceive me later in life.

My teenage years were by far my hardest. I became painfully self-conscious and increasingly aware that I was different. I struggled with swimming lessons because I was worried about wearing a swimsuit, and during the summer I’d wear clothes that kept me covered because I was embarrassed about how I looked. I wore thick foundation on my face to cover the patches around my eyes and mouth, and excessive layers of fake tan on my body. My skin had complete control of my life.

But one day, I realised I could take a very different and extremely liberating approach.

Speaking in Washington meanwhile, left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and former Trump adviser Steve Bannon have both called for greater governance of AI.

highlights.title: We don’t need AI regulation — leave safety to us, Nvidia’s Jensen Huang says
highlights.summary: AI isn't some new form of "alien mind," according to Jensen Huang. It's just hardware and software, so safety can be engineered by each AI product maker.
body: Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang made his position on the dangers AI poses very clear while speaking at Salesforce’s Dreamforce conference on Tuesday. To him, AI isn’t some new form of “alien mind,” as at least one OpenAI safety researcher has described it. It’s just hardware and software, he says, built by humans. That means, in his view, it can be controlled by humans and existing laws.

“Safety is an engineering problem, not a legal one,” he said. “We’re developing software after all. We’re developing computing systems after all. It’s a complicated computing system, but it’s ultimately a computing system.”

Therefore, there’s no need for new laws or regulations to govern it, he argues. In fact, Huang sees little need for new laws at all. The free market, he argues, will be enough to pressure companies not to release unsafe products.

“If we’re not confident about the safety of the products, like all companies, like you and I, all the companies here, if you build a product or a service, and you’re not confident in its functionality, capability, or safety, then don’t release it. And so that’s a very obvious thing to do,” he said.

Sixteen players joined Donald and his vice-captains for the team session ahead of travelling onto the DP World Tour's BMW PGA Championship - 10 of last year's line-up, two more with past Ryder Cup pedigree and four potential debutants.

highlights.title: Squid ink tomato pasta and honey and fig semifreddo: Chris Leach’s Italian recipes for the end of summer
highlights.summary: Cooking at this time of year is all about low-effort, maximum-impact options. This savoury dish comes together quickly but looks striking, while the dessert showcases figs at their most flavoursome.
body: The secret to late-summer/early autumn cooking is to keep things relatively low-effort, not least to assuage those back-to-work/school blues. And that rule applies across the board, whether you’re making a midweek meal, entertaining or serving up a long, slow Sunday lunch. The sauce for this pasta dish, for example, comes together while the pasta is cooking, while the semifreddo pudding makes the most of ripe figs when they are at their absolute best.
The contrast between the black pasta, the red tomatoes and the golden crumbs is really something else, as are the flavours.

First make the pangrattato. Tear the stale bread into rough pieces, then pulse in a food processor to make coarse, uneven breadcrumbs. Put the oil in a large frying pan on a medium heat, add the sliced garlic and cook gently, stirring, for a minute or two, until fragrant but not coloured. Add the thyme leaves, cook for a further 30 seconds, then stir in the breadcrumbs and cook, stirring regularly, for eight to 10 minutes, until evenly golden and crisp all over. Season with a pinch of sea salt and a little black pepper, then transfer to a plate to cool completely.

highlights.title: AI ‘Actor’ Tilly Norwood Told Me That ‘All Lives Matter’
highlights.summary: The virtual character, which is promoting its upcoming movie Misaligned, tries to evade politics by repetitively commenting on the clothes you’re wearing.
body: For Hollywood stars, press junkets are an opportunity to promote new work while connecting with fans. They tell funny or embarrassing stories about one another, give us a glimpse into the film production process, and reveal mannerisms that make them more relatable.

So why would anyone want to talk to Tilly Norwood, an interactive, British-accented digital character and “actor” developed with generative artificial intelligence by Xicoia, an AI division of a studio called Particle 6 Group? It’s a fair enough question considering that it does not exist in our physical realm and will never appear in a movie that any halfway serious person would care about.

But Particle 6 recently claimed in an email that Norwood was “ready for absolutely anything!” What’s more, the company is allowing journalists access to the model without a handler to “keep the conversation on track.” So I decided to test whether Norwood could actually offer anything of substance.
points: The virtual character, which is promoting its upcoming movie Misaligned, tries to evade politics by repetitively commenting on the clothes you’re wearing.

highlights.title: When did football fans first start wearing replica kits? | The Knowledge
highlights.summary: Plus: more costly (and beneficial) red cards, plus attacks with triple half-century of international goals. Mail us with your all of your questions and answers. “When did fans wearing replica kits become a thing?” asks Alex Ecob.
body: As the question suggests, this is a not a straightforward answer. Buckle up folks, as we veer wildly from copyright acts to academia, via multiple reports of unofficial kits, DIY jobs, cup-final special editions, youth strips, sew-on jobs and the like. But if we are to draw a line in the sand, and declare one date or one jersey as the first official, adult replica kit to be sold by a club to the general public (or at least those close enough to the club shop), then we probably have to give the gong to Leeds United in 1973, although only children’s sizes were produced initially.

“The first replica kit was produced by Admiral for Leeds United in 1973-74,” emails Chai from Atlanta. “History has it that Leeds’ manager, Don Revie, and Admiral owner, Bert Patrick, had a chance meeting at a cafe. There they agreed on Admiral paying Leeds £7,000 to wear a redesigned kit with the brand’s logo visible on their shirt and shorts. Patrick also secured the copyright to produce full replica kits for children, which sold for around £5.

highlights.title: 10 Darkest 'Calvin and Hobbes' Snowman Jokes That Reveal Bill Watterson's Twisted Genius
highlights.summary: Generally, when people think of Bill Watterson’s comic strip Calvin and Hobbes, they think of fun, innocent adventures with a little boy and his plush tiger, oftentimes exploring the woods or riding on a sled in the snow.
body: Calvin and Hobbes began on Nov. 18, 1985. While Watterson drew comic strips featuring snowmen in the first few years, on Feb. 28, 1988, he took a noticeably darker turn when he depicted a crowd of snowmen around the family car, as though there’d been a car accident. The beauty of the comic is the slow-burn, with Calvin seemingly-innocently making snowmen. Finally, in the last panel, the gruesome scene is revealed with his parents observing the scene, with Calvin’s dad saying, “I think we’d better get that kid to a psychologist.”

It would be almost a year before Watterson would go similarly dark with Calvin’s snowman sculptures, which is when it became a regular recurring series until the comic strip ended in 1995. Many of the strips featured death and destruction, even disturbing jokes about suicide that make you wonder how Calvin knew about this stuff. Some of the images were likely shocking, especially when juxtaposed against lighter comics like Peanuts or The Family Circus, but thanks to the multi-faceted personality Watterson crafted for Calvin, the dark jokes suited the character perfectly.
Here are the 10 darkest snowman gags that ever appeared in Calvin and Hobbes.

highlights.title: ‘Vivant’ Tops Asia Streaming Chart, First Japanese Drama to Lead, Report Finds
highlights.summary: TBS drama “Vivant” outdrew every other streaming title across Asia last month, excluding China and India, becoming the first Japanese show to top ampd Analytics’ regional monthly ranking since the measurement firm began tracking the market.
body: The finding comes from a new ampd Vision report titled “Vivant: A TV Broadcast Hit, Streamed.”

Beyond the streaming platforms, “Vivant” built a substantial following on YouTube, where related content drew 13.2 million viewers, nearly matching its VOD reach. That audience was spread across more than 1,600 videos posted by 450 channels, totaling 8.8 million hours watched at an average of almost 40 minutes per viewer. A companion show TBS produced alongside the drama, “Villains’ Meeting Room,” averaged more than 1.3 million viewers an episode.

The drama’s success did not extend much beyond Japan’s borders. Some 97% of all “Vivant” viewing came from local audiences, ampd found, a pattern consistent with Japanese dramas’ broader struggles abroad: they land in Netflix’s global top 10 outside Japan just 0.3 times a month on average, well behind Korean dramas at 4.1 times and Japanese anime at 1.4.

highlights.title: The girl with a will to live: the love, hope and pain of raising Elsie – my one in 163 million daughter
highlights.summary: She was born with an ultra-rare genetic disorder. After my decades working in film PR, I now face the biggest campaign of all: the fight for her life. My daughter Elsie has beautiful curls – blond like a little Botticelli cherub’s, hair that someone dark like me could only ever dream of.
body: Sound is important for Elsie because she has a visual impairment and, while we know she has some peripheral vision, is legally classed as blind. As a result, she uses her tongue to check her environment. When she’s excited it sticks out, tasting the air around her, licking anyone close, sensing space. And when she likes the taste of something she keeps her tongue out until you give her more. This is how we know she likes lollies.

She makes new sounds every day. If she suddenly realises she’s on her own, she’ll soon make her signature “Ah, ah!” sound until she’s got company again. But at 18 months she is behind in her development and we don’t yet know if she will be verbal, so for now we are learning to understand her in the ways she chooses to show us.

Elsie was born with a rare neurological condition – so rare that there are fewer than 100 known cases in the world. It is a mutation in the RARB (retinoic acid receptor beta) gene, which, when working properly, helps control vitamin A signalling, vital for the proper embryonic development of the eyes, brain, lungs and spinal cord. It is de novo (meaning it is not hereditary), and the effects are progressive.

highlights.title: Trails In The Sky 2nd Chapter Review
highlights.summary: An impressive remake which captures everything that made the original so endearing.
body: Trails in the Sky 2nd Chapter picks up right where its predecessor ends with our bubbly and confident heroine, Estelle Bright. Now that her adoptive brother and best friend Joshua Bright suddenly recalled his true origins and has disappeared, Estelle is dead set on finding him and bringing him home. It also digs deeper and fleshes out the cultish revelations that were unearthed towards the end of 1st Chapter. As a result, it gives 2nd Chapter heavier stakes from onset, but also with the emotionally resonant edge that keeps you invested.

2nd Chapter is virtually a faithful 1:1 recreation of the original in terms of story structure and side quests, so you’ll be running around Liberl Kingdom going through the same cities and locations as you did in 1st Chapter. While that might seem like a rehash, the order in which you visit them in this sequel is rearranged. Along with a completely different slate of side quests to tackle from the previous adventure, it makes this journey feel much less like a retread and more like revisiting an old home.
points: An impressive remake which captures everything that made the original so endearing.

body: Back in the autumn of 1973 a lighting system compatible with the demands of broadcasting in black and white was proving increasingly outdated and Sunderland responded by doubling admission prices for the second leg of their opening European Cup Winners’ Cup tie against Vasas of Budapest. Coming at a moment when miners and railway workers were engaged in long-running industrial action and north-easterners’ finances were duly tight, it dictated that a disappointing crowd of under 23,000 turned out to watch Dennis Tueart’s penalty secure a 3-0 aggregate win.

Fifty-three years on, Wearside’s financial outlook is once again uncertain as the gig economy makes security a stranger for many and the cost of living spirals, but a near 49,000-capacity crowd is still expected at the Stadium of Light on Wednesday night.
Sunderland’s opening Europa League match against AZ Alkmaar will be televised across much of the world in HD but if Granit Xhaka has his way, viewers may need to adjust their brightness controls.

highlights.title: New York Fashion Week’s Show-Stopping Season
highlights.summary: Unexpected attention was on NYFW, but for the discomfort and discourse, talent — both established and emerging — shone through.
body: Last night, New York Fashion Week (NYFW) came to a close with Thom Browne’s Spring/Summer 2027 collection, which he presented at the cavernous Hudson Yards venue The Shed, this time with a grassy garden set and metamorphosis theme. Browne, who is the chair of the board of the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA), typically shows just once per year in New York (though usually not in September), and the theatrics always deliver the right caliber of drama and artistry to end the week.

NYFW often gets chided for its predictability. Not so this season. An incident at Sunday’s Cos show — which involved CFDA CEO Steven Kolb physically interfering with Peta protestors — became the story of the week, as the video of the altercation circulated social media. By Monday afternoon, Kolb posted an apology to his Instagram Stories while the CFDA board released a statement saying that he will be on leave pending further review. Considering the future of one of NYFW’s leaders is up in the air, there was somewhat of a vibe shift as fashion week soldiered on in the midst of the media coverage that followed.
points: Unexpected attention was on NYFW, but for the discomfort and discourse, talent — both established and emerging — shone through.

highlights.title: How chimps teach their kids tool tricks
highlights.summary: Chimpanzees are known to use rudimentary tools when foraging for food. According to a new paper in the journal Frontiers in Psychology, this learned behavior is passed down from adults to offspring through social learning.
body: "Receiving food and tools from experienced individuals, which we call food or tool transfer, may help chimpanzees learn to use technology to extract foods that are difficult to access,” said co-author Andreu Sánchez-Megías, a graduate student at the University of Barcelona and the Jane Goodall Institute Spain in Senegal. “Tool transfers thus appear to be a form of teaching, together with observation and supervised practice. It appears that mothers are the main models and teachers for young chimpanzees in this manner.”

highlights.title: The AI data center boom is colliding with cities scarred by big industry
highlights.summary: National outcry against data center construction has spread to Philadelphia, where officials suggested possible construction in a neighborhood already impacted by a now-defunct oil refinery.
body: Across the country, Americans are debating how their lives might change if new AI data centers are built in their backyards. Data center companies and their customers are promising new jobs and economic growth, but that pitch hasn’t won over a majority of Americans who oppose data center construction in their area, often over environmental and energy concerns.
For activist Shawmar Pitts, these concerns aren’t theoretical. He knows better than anyone what it’s like to live in the shadow of American industrialization.

A lifelong resident of the Grays Ferry neighborhood in Southwest Philadelphia, Pitts grew up next to what was then the East Coast’s largest oil refinery, which shut down after an explosion in 2019. Though many of his friends and family suffered from chronic health conditions, he didn’t realize what might have caused these illnesses until he encountered the environmental justice group Philly Thrive, which was tabling in his neighborhood in 2018 about a proposed oil refinery expansion.

body: This week there was a return, however, to international action as Esteghlal and Tractor SC started out in the AFC Champions League Elite. It comes after the Persian Gulf League kicked off in mid-August, almost six months after it was postponed at the end of February, and subsequently abandoned as the war continued.

“The most important impact of the war on Iranian football was the prolonged suspension of competition,” the Esteghlal head coach, Sohrab Bakhtiarizadeh, says. “For months, we were deprived of club football, and not only were the players and teams unable to train, but the fans also had nothing to talk about, engage in banter over, and so on. It was sad that football was suspended for such a long period and it will certainly weaken the sport and its passionate supporters.”
